# 2 Chronicles 25 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Chapter

**Matthew Henry** (Presbyterian) divides the chapter into six sections: (I) Amaziah as a just avenger of his father's death (vv. 1–4); (II) an obedient observer of God's command (vv. 5–10); (III) a cruel conqueror of the Edomites (vv. 11–13); (IV) a foolish worshipper of Edom's gods, impatient of reproof (vv. 14–16); (V) rashly challenging Israel's king and suffering for it (vv. 17–24); (VI) ending his days ingloriously (vv. 25–28). — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-25-commentary

**Raymond Dillard** notes the Chronicler's record of Amaziah is overwhelmingly negative — a "study in opposites": instead of royal building, walls are destroyed; instead of wealth, plunder; instead of victory, defeat; instead of loyalty, conspiracy and regicide. The message for the post-exilic community was clear: exclusive loyalty to the covenant Lord is central. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-25-commentary

**Mark Boda** observes the Chronicler organizes Amaziah's reign into two parallel phases (positive vv. 5–12; negative vv. 13–24), each structured by the same six-step pattern: (1) action arousing God's anger; (2) prophetic confrontation; (3) Amaziah's question; (4) prophetic response; (5) obedience/disobedience; (6) success/failure in battle. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-25-commentary

**Martin Selman** says commentators disagree whether the reign has distinct favourable and unfavourable parts or whether Amaziah is fundamentally half-hearted throughout. Selman argues "he declines from bad to worse rather than from good to bad." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-25-commentary

---

## v. 1 — Amaziah's Age, Reign Length, and Mother

**Amaziah** means "Jehovah is mighty" or "strengthened by Jehovah." He was the eighth king of the separate kingdom of Judah, reigning c. 796–767 BC. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-25-commentary

**Pulpit Commentary** calculates that since Joash died at age 47 and Amaziah was 25, Amaziah was born when Joash was 22. Jehoaddan was likely one of the two wives Jehoiada selected for Joash. The affix "of Jerusalem" may honour Jehoiada for choosing a woman of the honoured city rather than a provincial one. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_chronicles/25.htm

**Precept Austin** notes that Amaziah's 29-year reign likely included a long co-regency: after Amaziah was captured by Jehoash of Israel (v. 23), his son Uzziah probably served as co-regent from about the fifth year, for some 24 years. Thiele dates the reign 796–767 BC. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-25-commentary

---

## v. 2 — "Right in the Eyes of the LORD, but Not Wholeheartedly"

**Guzik (Enduring Word)**: Compared to David, Amaziah did not match up favourably. The parallel in 2 Kings 14:1–4 shows he permitted continued high-place worship. G. Campbell Morgan: "The root idea of the Hebrew word translated 'perfect' [loyal] is being whole, complete. Imperfection of heart consists in incomplete surrender." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-25/

**Pulpit Commentary**: The "not perfect heart" is illustrated by his later idolatry (vv. 14–16, 20) and by what the parallel in 2 Kings 14:3–4 supplies — he did not suppress the high places. "In almost all cases, the not perfect heart speaks of that which began well, but did not 'endure unto the end.'" — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_chronicles/25.htm

**Ellicott**: The phrase "not with a perfect heart" is the Chronicler's brief equivalent of 2 Kings 14:3's longer statement. "The chronicler's estimate of both princes [Joash and Amaziah] is less favourable than that of the older historian. Such differences are perfectly natural, and it is needless to attempt to 'reconcile' or eliminate them." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/25.htm

**Matthew Henry (via Precept Austin)**: "He was not a man of serious piety or devotion himself, nor had he any zeal for the exercises of religion. He was no enemy to it, but a cool and indifferent friend. Such is the character of too many in this Laodicean age: they do that which is good, but not with the heart, not with a perfect heart." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-25-commentary

**NET Bible note**: The Hebrew reads "a complete heart" (לֵבָב שָׁלֵם). — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-25-commentary

**Haydock (Catholic)**: "Heart, and with perseverance." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/2-chronicles-25.html

**Dillard (via Precept Austin)**: While the Chronicler often divides reigns into obedient and disobedient periods, here he "depicts Amaziah as fundamentally halfhearted and mediocre from the beginning." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-25-commentary

---

## vv. 3–4 — Justice on the Assassins, but Mercy to Their Children

**Guzik**: Executing his father's murderers was both just and in Amaziah's own best interest — eliminating those who thought assassinating a king was a reasonable political tool. It also fulfilled Genesis 9:5–7 (the command to punish murderers). Sparing their children showed "some faith and courage" (Poole), since it was the standard practice of the ancient Near East to execute entire families. Amaziah obeyed Deuteronomy 24:16 instead. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-25/

**Gill**: Amaziah "did as it is written in the Law in the Book of Moses." This was a remarkable departure from custom; he restrained himself to the Mosaic command. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-25.html

**Matthew Henry**: "Though we should suppose they intended to avenge on their king the death of the prophet (as was intimated, 2 Chr. 24:25), yet this would by no means justify their wickedness; for they were not the avengers, but presumptuously took God's work out of his hands." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-25-commentary

**Constable**: Amaziah followed the Mosaic Law faithfully in this instance (Deut. 24:16), and the Chronicler selected this event as one of three key episodes to teach spiritual lessons. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-25.html (excerpt; full page not fetched)

**Bullinger**: Notes the parallel passage in 2 Kings 14:5–6. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bul/2-chronicles-25.html

---

## v. 5 — Amaziah Musters Judah's Army: 300,000 Men

**Gill**: Amaziah divided the people by families into thousands and hundreds with appointed captains. He numbered men from twenty years old and upward (the usual military age; Josephus says to age 50). The number 300,000 shows a great decrease since Jehoshaphat's time (2 Chr. 17:14 — over 1.1 million), "occasioned by the wars under Jehoram, Ahaziah, and Joash." Some Vulgate manuscripts read only 30,000. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-25.html

**Expositor's Bible Commentary**: The muster-roll shows how the sins of recent wicked reigns had reduced Judah. Jehoshaphat commanded over 1,160,000; Amaziah has only 300,000. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/2-chronicles-25.html

**Matthew Henry**: "Sin weakens a people, diminishes them, dispirits them, and lessens their number and figure." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-25-commentary

---

## v. 6 — Hiring 100,000 Israelite Mercenaries for 100 Talents of Silver

**Guzik**: Hiring mercenaries was common in the ancient world. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-25/

**Gill**: Amaziah judged his own army insufficient. One hundred talents of silver amounted to about £35,300 sterling; Beckius calculates about five and a half florins per soldier. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-25.html

**Matthew Henry**: "If he had advised with any of his prophets before he did this, or had but considered how little any of his ancestors got by their alliances with Israel, he would not have had this to undo again. But rashness makes work for repentance." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-25-commentary

---

## vv. 7–8 — The Man of God's Warning

**Guzik**: An anonymous prophet warned Amaziah not to use the Israelite mercenaries. "Even though it made military sense…according to the word from God, it made no spiritual sense. This is because God has power to help and to overthrow. To fight with God is to receive His help; to fight against Him is to have God overthrow you." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-25/

**Gill**: The Jews (Seder Olam Rabba) claimed this "man of God" was Amaziah's brother, Amos, father of Isaiah — but Gill says "without foundation." The Targum renders "the LORD is not with Israel" as "the Word of the Lord is not their help." Regarding v. 8, Gill says some take the words as ironic ("go ahead, be strong — and see what happens"), while others read them seriously ("go alone without the hired troops, and fight boldly"). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-25.html

**Bullinger**: Notes v. 8 uses the figure of speech *Eironeia* (irony). Also points out that "not with Israel" is "the measure by which our alliances of all kinds should be tried." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bul/2-chronicles-25.html

**Haydock (Catholic)**: The prophet speaks ironically. "Amasias ought to have known that no dependance was to be placed on Israel, while they despised God" (cf. 2 Chr. 15:2). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/2-chronicles-25.html

**Expositor's Bible Commentary**: "Jehovah, however, arrested Amaziah's employment of unholy allies at the outset." The chronicler carefully explains "Israel" means specifically "the children of Ephraim," so as not to seem blasphemous to his post-exilic contemporaries by saying God was not with all Israel. This hiring of Israelite troops was "the sin for which Jehoshaphat had twice been reproved and punished." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/2-chronicles-25.html

---

## v. 9 — "What about the Hundred Talents?" / "The LORD Can Give You Much More"

**Guzik**: Amaziah's question is the familiar one: "How much will it cost me to be obedient?" The prophet's answer: whatever obedience costs, it's always ultimately cheaper than disobedience. F.B. Meyer: "But you say that you have already entered into so close an alliance that you cannot draw back. You have invested your capital, you have gone to great expenditure. Yet it will be better to forfeit these than Him." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-25/

**Pulpit Commentary**: "This verse is consummate in the two touches by which it sets forth the phase of earth's calculatingness respecting the perishable, and Heaven's swift disposal of any such trifling difficulty." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_chronicles/25.htm

**MacLaren (Baptist preacher)**: This is his centrepiece sermon text. He calls Amaziah's question "a misplaced question" — not wrong in itself, but wrong in timing: duty must come first, consequences second. "Amaziah's first business should have been to see clearly what was duty; and then, and not till then, the next business should have been to consider consequences." MacLaren applies this to business ethics, church reform, and national policy. The triumphant answer: God gives "much more" — not necessarily more money, but character, Christ-likeness, and "durable riches." "He that wins strength and Christ-likeness of character by sacrificing for Christ has won far more than he can ever lose." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mac/2-chronicles-25.html

**Sermon Bible Commentary**: Three principles: (1) Where duty leads, go — whatever the painful consequences — and leave consequences with God. (2) Do this humbly, relying on God's grace. (3) "In the long run no man will ever lose by obeying God's bidding; and, just as assuredly, no man will ever gain by disobeying it." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/sbc/2-chronicles-25.html

**Matthew Henry**: "A firm belief of God's all-sufficiency to bear us out in our duty, and to make up all the loss and damage we sustain in his service abundantly to our advantage, will make his yoke very easy and his burden very light." Henry notes the exact sum of 100 talents was later given to Amaziah's grandson Jotham as a present (2 Chr. 27:5) — "then the principal was repaid, and, for interest, 10,000 measures of wheat and as many of barley." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-25-commentary

---

## v. 10 — Amaziah Dismisses the Ephraimite Troops; Their Anger

**Guzik**: Amaziah paid them as promised and sent them home in faith. Their anger "was greatly aroused…probably because they counted on the anticipated plunder as additional income." Selman: "The Israelites' great rage, repeated in Hebrew for emphasis, shows further why the Lord is not with them." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-25/

**Gill**: The Israelites were angered at the "great slight put upon them, and a reproach to them, to be thus dismissed…especially if they understood that it was because they were idolaters; and the rather as they might have hoped to have had their share in the plunder of the Edomites." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-25.html

---

## vv. 11–12 — Victory over Edom at the Valley of Salt

**Guzik**: Walking in obedience (having dismissed the mercenaries), Amaziah saw the victory God promised. Selman notes: "His victory is definite enough, though it is achieved without any acknowledgment of God's help and with excessive violence." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-25/

**Gill**: "Amaziah strengthened himself, and led forth his people…not discouraged by the dismission of the hired troops, but trusting in the promise and power of God." The "Valley of Salt" is south of the Dead Sea. Regarding the execution of 10,000 captives by throwing them from a rock (v. 12), Gill notes this was likely the rock on which Petra (the Edomite capital) was built — the Hebrew name *Selah* also means "rock." Gill calls the treatment "cruel and barbarous; and what should be the reason of such treatment of them is not easy to say." He compares it to Roman execution from the Tarpeian Rock and the Delphian law in Greece for sacrilege. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-25.html

**Bullinger**: The "Valley of Salt" is south of the Dead Sea; "children of Seir" = Edomites. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bul/2-chronicles-25.html

**Peake's Commentary**: The account of casting captives from a rock is compared to Psalm 141:6. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/2-chronicles-25.html

---

## v. 13 — Dismissed Mercenaries Raid Judah

**Guzik**: The Israelite soldiers, hungry for plunder, raided cities from Samaria to Beth-horon, killing 3,000. Poole suggests the 100 talents had been paid only to officers to raise troops, not distributed to all — so the soldiers felt cheated of spoil. F.B. Meyer: "Sin may be forgiven, but its secondary results are sometimes very bitter." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-25/

**Haydock (Catholic)**: The mercenaries went to Samaria to complain to King Joash, and "receiving no redress, began to plunder, as far as Bethhoron the lower." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/2-chronicles-25.html

**Matthew Henry**: "But why should God suffer this to be done? Was it not in obedience to him that they were sent home, and yet shall the country thus suffer by it? Surely God's way is in the sea! … Doubtless God intended hereby to chastise those cities of Judah for their idolatries, which were found most in those parts that lay next to Israel. The men of Israel had corrupted them, and now they were made a plague to them. Satan both tempts and torments." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-25-commentary

---

## v. 14 — Amaziah Worships the Gods of the Edomites He Defeated

**Guzik**: This shows "the deep foolishness of idolatry." These gods couldn't defend the Edomites, yet Amaziah worshipped them. Selman: "Amaziah's achievement seems to bring out the worst in him." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-25/

**Gill**: "Which was the greatest piece of sottishness and stupidity imaginable, to worship the gods of a nation conquered by him; for since they could not save them, what help could he expect from them?" Gill notes Josephus mentions "the priests of Coze, which he says was a god of the Idumaeans." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-25.html

**Peake's Commentary**: This account of Amaziah's idolatry has no parallel in 2 Kings; it is perhaps the Chronicler's own addition to explain why Judah was later defeated (vv. 17–24). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/2-chronicles-25.html

**Constable**: Idolatry struck at the heart of the covenant relationship. To turn from the living God to dead idols was "the height of effrontery (cf. Exodus 20:5)." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-25.html (excerpt)

---

## vv. 15–16 — The Prophet's Rebuke and Amaziah's Arrogant Reply

**Guzik**: The prophet's simple logic: "Why have you sought the gods…which could not rescue their own people from your hand?" Amaziah's response — "Have we made you the king's counselor? Cease! Why should you be killed?" — is arrogant rejection of God's mercy. Trapp: "When he might have sent him to hell with a thunderbolt; as the patientest man upon earth would have done likely, had he been in God's place and power." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-25/

**Gill**: The prophet was "not indeed one of his privy council, made so by him, but he was appointed a counsellor to him by the Lord, the King of kings." The king threatens death; the prophet "forbore" but added a final word: "I know that God hath determined to destroy thee…because thou hast done this; committed such idolatry, and persisted in it: and hast not hearkened to my counsel; to reform from it." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-25.html

**Haydock (Catholic)**: The prophet's authority as prophet "authorized him to give counsel even to kings. Amasias had perhaps obeyed this prophet, (v. 7) but now his heart was puffed up with victory." The threat "Why should you be killed?" was fulfilled "sixteen years hence" — a delayed but certain judgment. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/2-chronicles-25.html

---

## vv. 17–19 — Amaziah Challenges Jehoash of Israel; The Parable of the Thistle and Cedar

**Guzik**: Proud from success against Edom and retaliating for the mercenaries' raids, Amaziah challenged Israel. He had reason: his 300,000-man army had just killed 20,000 Edomites, while Jehoash of Israel seemed weak (only 50 horsemen, 10 chariots, and 10,000 foot soldiers after Syrian defeats — 2 Kings 13:7). Jehoash's reply with the parable of the thistle and cedar was "both wise and diplomatic." Dilday: "The thistle, imagining himself to be equal with the cedar, presumptuously suggested a marriage alliance between them. The difference between the two was made obvious when a wild beast passed through and crushed the thistle underfoot." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-25/

**Bullinger**: "Thistle = thorn. Compare 2 Kings 14:9." Also notes Amaziah "took man's counsel, but not God's" — a play on the word "counsel/advice" used in v. 16. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bul/2-chronicles-25.html

**Haydock (Catholic)**: "This fable insinuated how much Joas despised the insolence of his antagonist, and Amasias had soon reason to repent." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/2-chronicles-25.html

---

## v. 20 — "It Came from God" — Divine Hardening

**Guzik**: "Because of Amaziah's foolish embrace of idolatry, God allowed him to enter into a foolish war with Israel. Foolish idols led him into foolish choices, and the wise God in heaven allowed him to experience the effect of these choices." Poole: "It came of God, who gave him up to his own error and passion, in order to his ruin." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-25/

**Peake's Commentary**: This is an addition by the Chronicler to tie Amaziah's defeat directly to his idolatry (cf. vv. 14f). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/2-chronicles-25.html

**Haydock (Catholic)**: The Protestant rendering is noted: "it came of God, that he might deliver them into the hand of their enemies, because they sought after the gods of Edom." Haydock explains: "The king was permitted to give ear to evil counsellors. … 'Jupiter deprives those of understanding, whom he means to destroy.' — Homer. The heart is hardened on account of former sins." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/2-chronicles-25.html

---

## vv. 21–24 — Defeat at Beth-shemesh, Jerusalem's Wall Breached, Temple Plundered

**Guzik**: Amaziah lost his freedom (taken prisoner), Jerusalem's defenses (wall broken down 400 cubits from Ephraim Gate to Corner Gate), and the temple/royal treasures. Guzik stresses the communal cost: "The decision to attack Israel was his alone, but the price paid for the foolish attack was paid by the whole kingdom of Judah. It is a sober warning to all leaders." Clarke: "The quarrel of Amaziah was certainly just, yet he was put to the rout; he did meddle to his hurt; he fell, and Judah fell with him, as Jehoash had said." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-25/

**Gill**: Jehoash took "all the gold and silver, all the articles found in the house of God with Obed-Edom." — These were the temple treasures under the care of Obed-Edom and his family (1 Chr. 26:15). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-25.html

**Bullinger**: "Obed-edom. He and his family were the Temple treasurers (1 Chronicles 26:15). Hostages. Hebrew 'sons of securities.'" — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bul/2-chronicles-25.html

**Peake's Commentary**: The reference to Obed-Edom is an addition by the Chronicler (see 1 Chr. 26:15). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/2-chronicles-25.html

**John Olley (via Precept Austin)**: "His father's reign had begun with the joyful refurbishment of the temple, but Amaziah's was to be marked by the seizing of 'all the gold and silver, and all the vessels that were found in the house of God' (2Ch 25:24)." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-25-commentary

**Haydock (Catholic)**: Notes the "hostages" (Protestant rendering); the Hebrew literally means "sons of securities" — hostages taken to Samaria. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/2-chronicles-25.html

---

## vv. 25–26 — Amaziah Lives 15 More Years; the Royal Annals

**Guzik**: Amaziah lived 15 years after Jehoash's death (which probably prompted his release from captivity in Israel). Trapp: "But it was a kind of a lifeless life…. He lay all the while under the hatred and contempt of his subjects." Payne: "At a preliminary stage his sixteen-year-old son Uzziah was elevated to coregency – and to actual rule – in 790 B.C." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-25/

**Precept Austin**: The 15 years after Jehoash's death is a unique chronological note; it supports the theory that Amaziah was held hostage in Samaria until Jehoash died, then returned or shared power with his son Uzziah (already co-regent). — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-25-commentary

**Bullinger**: v. 26 uses the figure of speech *Erotesis* (rhetorical question) — "are they not written…?" — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bul/2-chronicles-25.html

---

## vv. 27–28 — Conspiracy, Flight to Lachish, and Assassination

**Guzik**: The embarrassing loss undermined Amaziah's support. He fled to Lachish but was followed and killed — assassinated just like his father (2 Kings 12:20–21). Knapp: "Lachish was the first of the cities of Judah to adopt the idolatries of the kingdom of Israel (Micah 1:13), and it was natural for the idolatrous Amaziah to seek an asylum there." Clarke: "He who forsook the Lord was forsaken by every friend, perished in his gainsaying, and came to an untimely end." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-25/

**Pulpit Commentary**: The phrase "upon the horses" (Hebrew: "upon the horses") probably refers to the royal horses with which he had fled. "This seems the most natural suggestion…and may indicate that they visited him with no additional gratuitous disrespect." The phrase "City of Judah" is probably a textual error for "City of David" (as in 2 Kings 14:20), found in some manuscripts. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_chronicles/25.htm

**Peake's Commentary**: "The conspiracy here referred to may well have taken place owing to the discontent which Amaziah's disastrous policy must have occasioned." The reference to Amaziah's falling away from Yahweh is again the Chronicler's own editorial comment. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/2-chronicles-25.html

**Bullinger**: Notes the figure *Polyptoton* in v. 27: "conspired a great conspiracy" — Hebrew repetition for emphasis. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bul/2-chronicles-25.html

**Constable**: "From the time Amaziah turned from Yahweh, God began to turn against him by using the faithful in Judah as His instruments of judgment." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-25.html (excerpt)

---

## Protestant Traditions: Distinctive Emphases

### Reformed / Presbyterian
The **Pulpit Commentary** emphasises the covenantal framework: Amaziah began well but did not endure, illustrating the persevering grace required. Matthew Henry applies the "not wholehearted" diagnosis to "this Laodicean age." The **Expositor's Bible Commentary** underscores the sin of seeking "unholy allies" — a Reformed emphasis on trusting God alone rather than worldly alliances.

### Baptist
**MacLaren** (Baptist preacher, 1904) builds his entire sermon on v. 9 — the "misplaced question" of counting the cost before determining duty. He applies it pointedly to Christians who hesitate to take a firm stand because of business or social cost. He also notably challenges state-church establishments: "one great argument that our friends who believe in an Established Church are always bringing forward, is just a modern form of Amaziah's question." **Gill** (Baptist) focuses on historical and linguistic detail, noting the decline in Judah's manpower as divine chastening.

### Pentecostal / Charismatic
**Enduring Word** (David Guzik, charismatic-leaning evangelical) emphasises the faith dimension: Amaziah sent the mercenaries home "in faith, trusting God to both protect and provide." The commentary stresses the spiritual principle that God can give "much more" — and the practical warning that leaders' foolish decisions hurt many others.

### Evangelical (broadly)
**Precept Austin** compiles multiple evangelical sources (Dillard, Selman, Olley, Boda, Utley). The repeated emphasis is that partial obedience is disobedience, and that God evaluates the heart (*Coram Deo*). **Constable** (Dallas Theological Seminary) structures the chapter as three key events teaching spiritual lessons about law-keeping, trust in God, and the consequences of idolatry.

### Methodist / Wesleyan / Holiness
The **Sermon Bible Commentary** and **Church Pulpit Commentary** stress the "weighing of consequences" as a practical matter of holy living: "The grand thing is, not that a man should say that he will go on in the path of duty, whatever loss that may bring him, but that those around him should see that he is going on in the path of duty, though that should not be the path of worldly gain." This reflects the Holiness tradition's emphasis on visible, consistent Christian conduct.

---

## Other Views

### Catholic Reading
**Haydock's Catholic Bible Commentary** (1811) follows the traditional reading closely. Notable points: the prophet in v. 8 speaks ironically; Amaziah's heart was hardened "on account of former sins" — a Catholic emphasis on the progression of sin leading to judicial hardening. Haydock notes that God "permitted" Amaziah to follow evil counsellors. The fable of the thistle is "a fable" demonstrating Joash's contempt. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/2-chronicles-25.html

### Modern Scholarship
**Peake's Commentary** identifies vv. 5–10 as "a midrashic expansion of 2 Kings 14:7" — the Chronicler's creative theological elaboration. The idolatry account (vv. 14–16) "has no parallel in 2 K.; it is perhaps the work of the Chronicler, who added it in order to give a reason for the defeat." The reference to Amaziah "turning from following the LORD" (v. 27) is "again due to the Chronicler." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/2-chronicles-25.html
